{{Short description|Partial results found before the complete proof}}
[[Fermat's Last Theorem]] is a theorem in [[number theory]], originally stated by [[Pierre de Fermat]] in 1637 and [[Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem|proven]] by [[Andrew Wiles]] in 1995.  The statement of the theorem involves an [[integer]] [[exponent]] {{math|''n''}} larger than 2.  In the centuries following the initial statement of the result and before its general proof, various proofs were devised for particular values of the exponent {{math|''n''}}.  Several of these proofs are described below, including Fermat's proof in the case {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}}, which is an early example of the method of [[infinite descent]].

==Mathematical preliminaries==

Fermat's Last Theorem states that no three [[positive integer]]s {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} can satisfy the equation {{math|''a''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''b''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''c''<sup>''n''</sup>}} for any integer value of {{math|''n''}} greater than 2.  (For {{math|''n''}} equal to 1, the equation is a [[linear equation]] and has a solution for every possible {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}}.  For {{math|''n''}} equal to 2, the equation has infinitely many solutions, the [[Pythagorean triple]]s.)

===Factors of exponents===

A solution {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} for a given {{math|''n''}} leads to a solution for all the factors of {{math|''n''}}: if {{math|''h''}} is a factor of {{math|''n''}} then there is an integer {{math|''g''}} such that {{math|''n'' {{=}} ''gh''}}.  Then {{math|(''a''<sup>''g''</sup>, ''b''<sup>''g''</sup>, ''c''<sup>''g''</sup>)}} is a solution for the exponent {{math|''h''}}:

: {{math|(''a''<sup>''g''</sup>)<sup>''h''</sup> + (''b''<sup>''g''</sup>)<sup>''h''</sup> {{=}} (''c''<sup>''g''</sup>)<sup>''h''</sup>}}.

Therefore, to prove that Fermat's equation has ''no'' solutions for {{math|''n'' > 2}}, it suffices to prove that it has no solutions for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}} and for all odd primes {{math|''p''}}.

For any such odd exponent {{math|''p''}}, every positive-integer solution of the equation {{math|''a''<sup>''p''</sup> + ''b''<sup>''p''</sup> {{=}} ''c''<sup>''p''</sup>}} corresponds to a general integer solution to the equation {{math|''a''<sup>''p''</sup> + ''b''<sup>''p''</sup> + ''c''<sup>''p''</sup> {{=}} 0}}.  For example, if {{math|(3, 5, 8)}} solves the first equation, then {{math|(3, 5, −8)}} solves the second.  Conversely, any solution of the second equation corresponds to a solution to the first.  The second equation is sometimes useful because it makes the symmetry between the three variables {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}} and {{math|''c''}} more apparent.

===Primitive solutions===

If two of the three numbers {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} can be divided by a fourth number {{math|''d''}}, then all three numbers are divisible by {{math|''d''}}.  For example, if {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''c''}} are divisible by {{math|''d'' {{=}} 13}}, then {{math|''b''}} is also divisible by 13.  This follows from the equation

: {{math|''b''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''c''<sup>''n''</sup> − ''a''<sup>''n''</sup>}}

If the right-hand side of the equation is divisible by 13, then the left-hand side is also divisible by 13.  Let {{math|''g''}} represent the [[greatest common divisor]] of {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, and {{math|''c''}}.  Then {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} may be written as {{math|''a'' {{=}} ''gx''}}, {{math|''b'' {{=}} ''gy''}}, and {{math|''c'' {{=}} ''gz''}} where the three numbers {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} are pairwise [[coprime]].  In other words, the greatest common divisor ({{math|GCD}}) of each pair equals one

:{{math|GCD(''x'', ''y'') {{=}} GCD(''x'', ''z'') {{=}} GCD(''y'', ''z'') {{=}} 1}}

If {{math|(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} is a solution of Fermat's equation, then so is {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}}, since the equation

:{{math|''a''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''b''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''c''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''g''<sup>''n''</sup>''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''g''<sup>''n''</sup>''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''g''<sup>''n''</sup>''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}}

implies the equation

: {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}}.

A pairwise coprime solution {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} is called a ''primitive solution''.   Since every solution to Fermat's equation can be reduced to a primitive solution by dividing by their greatest common divisor ''g'', Fermat's Last Theorem can be proven by demonstrating that no primitive solutions exist.

===Even and odd===

Integers can be divided into even and odd, those that are evenly divisible by two and those that are not.  The even integers are {{math|...−4, −2, 0, 2, 4,...}} whereas the odd integers are {{math|...−3, −1, 1, 3,...}}.  The property of whether an integer is even (or not) is known as its [[parity (mathematics)|parity]].  If two numbers are both even or both odd, they have the same parity.  By contrast, if one is even and the other odd, they have different parity.

The addition, subtraction and multiplication of even and odd integers obey simple rules.  The addition or subtraction of two even numbers or of two odd numbers always produces an even number, e.g., {{math|4 + 6 {{=}} 10}} and {{math|3 + 5 {{=}} 8}}.  Conversely, the addition or subtraction of an odd and even number is always odd, e.g., {{math|3 + 8 {{=}} 11}}.  The multiplication of two odd numbers is always odd, but the multiplication of an even number with any number is always even.  An odd number raised to a power is always odd and an even number raised to power is always even, so for example ''x''<sup>''n''</sup> has the same parity as ''x''.

Consider any primitive solution {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} to the equation {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''n''</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}}. The terms in {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} cannot all be even, for then they would not be coprime; they could all be divided by two.  If {{math|''x''<sup>''n''</sup>}} and {{math|''y''<sup>''n''</sup>}} are both even, {{math|''z''<sup>''n''</sup>}} would be even, so at least one of {{math|''x<sup>n</sup>''}} and {{math|''y''<sup>''n''</sup>}} are odd.  The remaining addend is either even or odd; thus, the parities of the values in the sum are either (odd + even = odd) or (odd + odd = even).

===Prime factorization===

The [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic]] states that any natural number can be written in only one way (uniquely) as the product of prime numbers.  For example, 42 equals the product of prime numbers {{math|2 × 3 × 7}}, and no other product of prime numbers equals 42, aside from trivial rearrangements such as {{math|7 × 3 × 2}}.  This unique factorization property is the basis on which much of [[number theory]] is built.

One consequence of this unique factorization property is that if a {{math|''p''}}th power of a number equals a product such as

: {{math|''x''<sup>''p''</sup> {{=}} ''uv''}}

and if {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} are coprime (share no prime factors), then {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} are themselves the {{math|''p''}}th power of two other numbers, {{math|''u'' {{=}} ''r''<sup>''p''</sup>}} and {{math|''v'' {{=}} ''s''<sup>''p''</sup>}}.

As described below, however, some number systems do not have unique factorization.  This fact led to the failure of Lamé's 1847 general proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

===Two cases===
{{main|Sophie Germain's theorem}}
Since the time of [[Sophie Germain]], Fermat's Last Theorem has been separated into two cases that are proven separately.  The first case (case I) is to show that there are no primitive solutions {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} to the equation {{math|''x''<sup>''p''</sup> + ''y''<sup>''p''</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>''p''</sup>}} under the condition that {{math|''p''}} does not divide the product {{math|''xyz''}}.  The second case (case II) corresponds to the condition that {{math|''p''}} does divide the product {{math|''xyz''}}.  Since {{math|''x''}}, {{math|''y''}}, and {{math|''z''}} are pairwise coprime, {{math|''p''}} divides only one of the three numbers.

=={{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}}==

[[File:Pierre de Fermat.png|thumb|Portrait of Pierre de Fermat.]]

Only one [[mathematical proof]] by Fermat has survived, in which Fermat uses the technique of [[infinite descent]] to show that the area of a right triangle with integer sides can never equal the square of an integer.<ref>{{cite web | author = Freeman L | title = Fermat's One Proof | url = https://fermatslasttheorem.blogspot.com/2005/05/fermats-one-proof.html | access-date = 2009-05-23}}</ref>  This result is known as [[Fermat's right triangle theorem]]. As shown below, his proof is equivalent to demonstrating that the equation

: {{math|''x''<sup>4</sup> − ''y''<sup>4</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>2</sup>}}

has no primitive solutions in integers (no pairwise coprime solutions).  In turn, this is sufficient to prove Fermat's Last Theorem for the case {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}}, since the equation {{math|''a''<sup>4</sup> + ''b''<sup>4</sup> {{=}} ''c''<sup>4</sup>}} can be written as {{math|''c''<sup>4</sup> − ''b''<sup>4</sup> {{=}} (''a''<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup>}}.  Alternative proofs of the case {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}} were developed later<ref>Ribenboim, pp. 15–24.</ref> by Frénicle de Bessy,<ref>Frénicle de Bessy, ''Traité des Triangles Rectangles en Nombres'', vol. ===Application to right triangles===

Fermat's proof demonstrates that no right triangle with integer sides can have an area that is a square.<ref name="Fermat_1637">Fermat P. "Ad Problema XX commentarii in ultimam questionem Arithmeticorum Diophanti. Area trianguli rectanguli in numeris non potest esse quadratus", ''Œuvres'', vol. I, p. 340 (Latin), vol. III, pp. 271–272 (French).  Paris:Gauthier-Villars, 1891, 1896.</ref>  Let the right triangle have sides {{math|(''u'', ''v'', ''w'')}}, where the area equals {{math|{{sfrac|''uv''|2}}}} and, by the [[Pythagorean theorem]], {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> + ''v''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''w''<sup>2</sup>}}.  If the area were equal to the square of an integer {{math|''s''}}

: {{math|{{sfrac|''uv''|2}} {{=}} ''s''<sup>2</sup>}}

then by algebraic manipulations it would also be the case that

: {{math|2''uv'' {{=}} 4''s''<sup>2</sup>}} and {{math|−2''uv'' {{=}} −4''s''<sup>2</sup>}}.

Adding {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> + ''v''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''w''<sup>2</sup>}} to these equations gives

: {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> + 2''uv'' + ''v''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''w''<sup>2</sup> + 4''s''<sup>2</sup>}} and {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> − 2''uv'' + ''v''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''w''<sup>2</sup> − 4''s''<sup>2</sup>}},

which can be expressed as

: {{math|(''u'' + ''v'')<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''w''<sup>2</sup> + 4''s''<sup>2</sup>}} and {{math|(''u'' − ''v'')<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''w''<sup>2</sup> − 4''s''<sup>2</sup>}}.

Multiplying these equations together yields

: {{math|(''u''<sup>2</sup> − ''v''<sup>2</sup>)<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''w''<sup>4</sup> − 16''s''<sup>4</sup>}}.

But as Fermat proved, there can be no integer solution to the equation {{math|''x''<sup>4</sup> − ''y''<sup>4</sup> {{=}} ''z''<sup>2</sup>}}, of which this is a special case with {{math|''z'' {{=}} ''u''<sup>2</sup> − ''v''<sup>2</sup>}}, {{math|''x'' {{=}} ''w''}} and {{math|''y'' {{=}} 2''s''}}.

The first step of Fermat's proof is to factor the left-hand side<ref>Ribenboim, pp. 11–14.</ref>

: {{math|(''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup>)(''x''<sup>2</sup> − ''y''<sup>2</sup>) {{=}} ''z''<sup>2</sup>}}

Since {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} are coprime (this can be assumed because otherwise the factors could be cancelled), the greatest common divisor of {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup>}} and {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup> − ''y''<sup>2</sup>}} is either 2 (case A) or 1 (case B).  The theorem is proven separately for these two cases.

===Proof for case A===

In this case, both {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} are odd and {{math|''z''}} is even.  Since {{math|(''y''<sup>2</sup>, ''z'', ''x''<sup>2</sup>)}} form a primitive Pythagorean triple, they can be written

: {{math|''z'' {{=}} 2''de''}}
: {{math|''y''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''d''<sup>2</sup> − ''e''<sup>2</sup>}}
: {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''d''<sup>2</sup> + ''e''<sup>2</sup>}}

where {{math|''d''}} and {{math|''e''}} are coprime and {{math|''d'' > ''e'' > 0}}.  Thus,

: {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup>''y''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''d''<sup>4</sup> − ''e''<sup>4</sup>}}

which produces another solution {{math|(''d'', ''e'', ''xy'')}} that is smaller ({{math|0 < ''d'' < ''x''}}).  As before, there must be a lower bound on the size of solutions, while this argument always produces a smaller solution than any given one, and thus the original solution is impossible.

===Proof for case B===

In this case, the two factors are coprime.  Since their product is a square {{math|''z''<sup>2</sup>}}, they must each be a square

: {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''s''<sup>2</sup>}}
: {{math|''x''<sup>2</sup> − ''y''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''t''<sup>2</sup>}}

The numbers {{math|''s''}} and {{math|''t''}} are both odd, since {{math|''s''<sup>2</sup> + ''t''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} 2''x''<sup>2</sup>}}, an even number, and since {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} cannot both be even.  Therefore, the sum and difference of {{math|''s''}} and {{math|''t''}} are likewise even numbers, so we define integers {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} as

: {{math|''u'' {{=}} {{sfrac|''s'' + ''t''|2}}}}
: {{math|''v'' {{=}} {{sfrac|''s'' − ''t''|2}}}}

Since {{math|''s''}} and {{math|''t''}} are coprime, so are {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}}; only one of them can be even.  Since {{math|''y''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} 2''uv''}}, exactly one of them is even.  For illustration, let {{math|''u''}} be even; then the numbers may be written as {{math|''u'' {{=}} 2''m''<sup>2</sup>}} and {{math|''v'' {{=}} ''k''<sup>2</sup>}}.  Since {{math|(''u'', ''v'', ''x'')}} form a primitive [[Pythagorean triple]]

:{{math|{{sfrac|''s''<sup>2</sup> + ''t''<sup>2</sup>|2}}  {{=}} ''u''<sup>2</sup> + ''v''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''x''<sup>2</sup>}}

they can be expressed in terms of smaller integers {{math|''d''}} and {{math|''e''}} using Euclid's formula

: {{math|''u'' {{=}} 2''de''}}
: {{math|''v'' {{=}} ''d''<sup>2</sup> − ''e''<sup>2</sup>}}
: {{math|''x'' {{=}} ''d''<sup>2</sup> + ''e''<sup>2</sup>}}

Since {{math|''u'' {{=}} 2''m''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} 2''de''}}, and since {{math|''d''}} and {{math|''e''}} are coprime, they must be squares themselves, {{math|''d'' {{=}} ''g''<sup>2</sup>}} and {{math|''e'' {{=}} ''h''<sup>2</sup>}}.  This gives the equation

: {{math|''v'' {{=}} ''d''<sup>2</sup> − ''e''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''g''<sup>4</sup> − ''h''<sup>4</sup> {{=}} ''k''<sup>2</sup>}}

The solution {{math|(''g'', ''h'', ''k'')}} is another solution to the original equation, but smaller ({{math|0 < ''g'' < ''d'' < ''x''}}).  Applying the same procedure to {{math|(''g'', ''h'', ''k'')}}  would produce another solution, still smaller, and so on.  But this is impossible, since natural numbers cannot be shrunk indefinitely.  Therefore, the original solution {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} was impossible.

=={{math|''n'' {{=}} 3}}==

[[File:Leonhard Euler.jpg|thumb|[[Leonhard Euler]] by [[Jakob Emanuel Handmann]].]]

Fermat sent the letters in which he mentioned the case in which {{math|''n'' {{=}} 3}} in 1636, 1640 and 1657.<ref name="Dickson_2005">{{Harvtxt|Dickson|2005|p=546}}</ref>
[[Leonhard Euler|Euler]] sent a letter to [[Christian Goldbach|Goldbach]] on 4 August 1753 in which claimed to have a proof of the case in which {{math|''n'' {{=}} 3}}.<ref name="Mactutor_1996" />
Euler had a complete and pure elementary proof in 1760, but the result was not published.<ref name="Bergmann_1966">{{Harvtxt|Bergmann|1966}}</ref>
Later,  [[Leonhard Euler|Euler's]] proof for  {{math|''n'' {{=}} 3}} was published in 1770.<ref name="Euler_1770">[[Leonhard Euler|Euler L]] (1770) ''Vollständige Anleitung zur Algebra'', Roy.Acad. As Fermat did for the case {{math|''n'' {{=}} 4}}, Euler used the technique of [[infinite descent]].<ref>Ribenboim, pp. 24–49.</ref> The proof assumes a solution {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} to the equation {{math|''x''<sup>3</sup> + ''y''<sup>3</sup> + ''z''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} 0}}, where the three non-zero integers {{math|''x''}}, {{math|''y''}}, and {{math|''z''}} are pairwise coprime and not all positive. One of the three must be even, whereas the other two are odd.  [[Without loss of generality]], {{math|''z''}} may be assumed to be even.

Since {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} are both odd, they cannot be equal.  If {{math|''x'' {{=}} ''y''}}, then {{math|2''x''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} −''z''<sup>3</sup>}}, which implies that {{math|''x''}} is even, a contradiction.

Since {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} are both odd, their sum and difference are both even numbers

:{{math|2''u'' {{=}} ''x'' + ''y''}}
:{{math|2''v'' {{=}} ''x'' − ''y''}}

where the non-zero integers {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} are coprime and have different parity (one is even, the other odd).  Since {{math|''x'' {{=}} ''u'' + ''v''}} and {{math|''y'' {{=}} ''u'' − ''v''}}, it follows that

:{{math|−''z''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} (''u'' + ''v'')<sup>3</sup> + (''u'' − ''v'')<sup>3</sup> {{=}} 2''u''(''u''<sup>2</sup> + 3''v''<sup>2</sup>)}}

Since {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} have opposite parity, {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> + 3''v''<sup>2</sup>}} is always an odd number.  Therefore, since {{math|''z''}} is even, {{math|''u''}} is even and {{math|''v''}} is odd.  Since {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} are coprime, the greatest common divisor of {{math|2''u''}} and {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> + 3''v''<sup>2</sup>}} is either 1 (case A) or 3 (case B).

===Proof for case A===

In this case,  the two factors of {{math|−''z''<sup>3</sup>}} are coprime. This implies that three does not divide {{math|''u''}} and that the two factors are cubes of two smaller numbers, {{math|''r''}} and {{math|''s''}}

: {{math|2''u'' {{=}} ''r''<sup>3</sup>}}
: {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> + 3''v''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''s''<sup>3</sup>}}

Since {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> + 3''v''<sup>2</sup>}} is odd, so is {{math|''s''}}.  A crucial lemma shows that if {{math|''s''}} is odd and if it satisfies an equation  {{math|''s''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} ''u''<sup>2</sup> + 3''v''<sup>2</sup>}}, then it can be written in terms of two integers {{math|''e''}} and {{math|''f''}}

: {{math|''s'' {{=}} ''e''<sup>2</sup> + 3''f''<sup>2</sup>}}

so that

: {{math|''u'' {{=}} ''e''(''e''<sup>2</sup> − 9''f''<sup>2</sup>)}}
: {{math|''v'' {{=}} 3''f''(''e''<sup>2</sup> − ''f''<sup>2</sup>)}}

{{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} are coprime, so {{math|''e''}} and {{math|''f''}} must be coprime, too. Since {{math|''u''}} is even and {{math|''v''}} odd, {{math|''e''}} is even and {{math|''f''}} is odd. Since

:  {{math|''r''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} 2''u'' {{=}} 2''e''(''e'' − 3''f'')(''e'' + 3''f'')}}

The factors {{math|2''e''}}, {{math|(''e'' – 3''f'')}}, and {{math|(''e'' + 3''f'')}} are coprime since 3 cannot divide {{math|''e''}}: if {{math|''e''}} were divisible by 3, then 3 would divide {{math|''u''}}, violating the designation of {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} as coprime. Since the three factors on the right-hand side are coprime, they must individually equal cubes of smaller integers

: {{math|−2''e'' {{=}} ''k''<sup>3</sup>}}
: {{math|''e'' − 3''f'' {{=}} ''l''<sup>3</sup>}}
: {{math|''e'' + 3''f'' {{=}} ''m''<sup>3</sup>}}

which yields a smaller solution {{math|''k''<sup>3</sup> + ''l''<sup>3</sup> + ''m''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} 0}}.  Therefore, by the argument of [[infinite descent]], the original solution {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}}  was impossible.

===Proof for case B===

In this case, the greatest common divisor of {{math|2''u''}} and {{math|''u''<sup>2</sup> + 3''v''<sup>2</sup>}} is 3. That implies that 3 divides {{math|''u''}}, and one may express {{math|''u'' {{=}} 3''w''}} in terms of a smaller integer, {{math|''w''}}.  Since {{math|''u''}} is divisible by 4, so is {{math|''w''}}; hence, {{math|''w''}} is also even. Since {{math|''u''}} and {{math|''v''}} are coprime, so are {{math|''v''}} and {{math|''w''}}.  Therefore, neither 3 nor 4 divide {{math|''v''}}.

Substituting {{math|''u''}} by {{math|''w''}} in the equation for {{math|''z''<sup>3</sup>}} yields

:{{math|−''z''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} 6''w''(9''w''<sup>2</sup> + 3''v''<sup>2</sup>) {{=}} 18''w''(3''w''<sup>2</sup> + ''v''<sup>2</sup>)}}

Because {{math|''v''}} and {{math|''w''}} are coprime, and because 3 does not divide {{math|''v''}}, then {{math|18''w''}} and {{math|3''w''<sup>2</sup> + ''v''<sup>2</sup>}} are also coprime.  Therefore, since their product is a cube, they are each the cube of smaller integers, {{math|''r''}} and {{math|''s''}}

: {{math|18''w'' {{=}} ''r''<sup>3</sup>}}
: {{math|3''w''<sup>2</sup> + ''v''<sup>2</sup> {{=}} ''s''<sup>3</sup>}}

By the lemma above, since {{math|''s''}} is odd and its cube is equal to a number of the form {{math|3''w''<sup>2</sup> + ''v''<sup>2</sup>}}, it too can be expressed in terms of smaller coprime numbers, {{math|''e''}} and {{math|''f''}}.

: {{math|''s'' {{=}} ''e''<sup>2</sup> + 3''f''<sup>2</sup>}}

A short calculation shows that

: {{math|''v'' {{=}} ''e''(''e''<sup>2</sup> − 9''f''<sup>2</sup>)}}
: {{math|''w'' {{=}} 3''f''(''e''<sup>2</sup> − ''f''<sup>2</sup>)}}

Thus, {{math|''e''}} is odd and {{math|''f''}} is even, because {{math|''v''}} is odd. The expression for {{math|18''w''}} then becomes

: {{math|''r''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} 18''w'' {{=}} 54''f''(''e''<sup>2</sup> − ''f''<sup>2</sup>) {{=}} 54''f''(''e'' + ''f'')(''e'' − ''f'') {{=}} 3<sup>3</sup> × 2''f''(''e'' + ''f'')(''e'' − ''f'')}}.

Since {{math|3<sup>3</sup>}} divides {{math|''r''<sup>3</sup>}} we have that 3 divides ''r'', so {{math|({{sfrac|''r''|3}})<sup>3</sup>}} is an integer that equals {{math|2''f''(''e'' + ''f'')(''e'' − ''f'')}}. Since {{math|''e''}} and {{math|''f''}} are coprime, so are the three factors {{math|2''f''}}, {{math|''e'' + ''f''}}, and {{math|''e'' − ''f''}}; therefore, they are each the cube of smaller integers, ''k'', ''l'', and ''m''.

: {{math|−2''f'' {{=}} ''k''<sup>3</sup>}}
: {{math|''e'' + ''f'' {{=}} ''l''<sup>3</sup>}}
: {{math|''f'' − ''e'' {{=}} ''m''<sup>3</sup>}}

which yields a smaller solution {{math|''k''<sup>3</sup> + ''l''<sup>3</sup> + ''m''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} 0}}.  Therefore, by the argument of [[infinite descent]], the original solution {{math|(''x'', ''y'', ''z'')}} was impossible.

=={{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}}==

[[File:Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet.jpg|thumb|right|Portrait of [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]].]]
[[File:Legendre.jpg|thumb|right|Caricature of [[Adrien-Marie Legendre]] (the only surviving portrait of him).]]

Fermat's Last Theorem for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}} states that no three coprime integers {{math|''x''}}, {{math|''y''}} and {{math|''z''}} can satisfy the equation

: {{math|''x''<sup>5</sup> + ''y''<sup>5</sup> + ''z''<sup>5</sup> {{=}} 0}}

This was proven<ref>{{cite web | author = Freeman L | title = Fermat's Last Theorem: Proof for ''n'' = 5 | url = https://fermatslasttheorem.blogspot.com/2005/10/fermats-last-theorem-proof-for-n5_28.html | access-date = 2009-05-23}}</ref> neither independently nor collaboratively by [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet|Dirichlet]] and [[Adrien-Marie Legendre|Legendre]] around 1825.<ref name="Mactutor_1996">{{Harvtxt|O'Connor|Robertson|1996}}</ref><ref>Ribenboim, p. 49.</ref>  Alternative proofs were developed<ref>Ribenboim, pp. 55–57.</ref> by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]],<ref>{{cite book | author = Gauss CF | author-link = Carl Friedrich Gauss | date = 1875 | chapter = Neue Theorie der Zerlegung der Cuben | title = Zur Theorie der complexen Zahlen, Werke, vol. II | edition = 2nd | publisher = Königl. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen | pages = 387–391}}</ref> [[Victor-Amédée Lebesgue|Lebesgue]],<ref>{{cite journal | author = Lebesgue VA | author-link = Victor Lebesgue | year = 1843 | title = Théorèmes nouveaux sur l'équation indéterminée ''x''<sup>5</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''y''<sup>5</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''az''<sup>5</sup> | journal = J. Math. Pures Appl. | volume = 8 | pages = 49–70}}</ref> [[Gabriel Lamé|Lamé]],<ref>{{cite journal | author = Lamé G | author-link = Gabriel Lamé | year = 1847 | title = Mémoire sur la résolution en nombres complexes de l'équation ''A''<sup>5</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''B''<sup>5</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''C''<sup>5</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 | journal = J. Math. Pures Appl. | volume = 12 | pages = 137–171}}</ref> Gambioli,<ref name="Gambioli_1901" /><ref>{{cite journal | author = Gambioli D | year = 1903–1904 | title = Intorno all'ultimo teorema di Fermat | journal = Il Pitagora | volume = 10 | pages = 11–13, 41–42}}</ref> Werebrusow,<ref>{{cite journal | author = Werebrusow AS | year = 1905 | title = On the equation ''x''<sup>5</sup> + ''y''<sup>5</sup> = ''Az''<sup>5</sup> ''(in Russian)'' | journal = Moskov. Math. Samml. | volume = 25 | pages = 466–473}}</ref> [[Karel Rychlík|Rychlik]],<ref>{{cite journal | author = Rychlik K | author-link = Karel Rychlík | year = 1910 | title = On Fermat's last theorem for ''n'' = 5 ''(in Bohemian)'' | journal = Časopis Pěst. Mat. | volume = 39 | pages =185–195, 305–317}}</ref>  [[Johannes van der Corput|van der Corput]],<ref name="van_der_Corput_1915" /> and [[Guy Terjanian|Terjanian]].<ref>{{cite journal | author = Terjanian G | author-link = Guy Terjanian | year = 1987 | title = Sur une question de V. A. Lebesgue | journal = Annales de l'Institut Fourier | volume = 37 | pages = 19–37 | doi = 10.5802/aif.1096 | issue = 3| doi-access = free }}</ref>

Dirichlet's proof for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}} is divided into the two cases (cases I and II) defined by [[Sophie Germain]].  In case I, the exponent 5 does not divide the product {{math|''xyz''}}.  In case II, 5 does divide {{math|''xyz''}}.

#[[#Two cases|Case I]] for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}} can be proven immediately by [[Sophie Germain's theorem]](1823) if the auxiliary prime {{math|''θ'' {{=}} 11}}.
#[[#Two cases|Case II]] is divided into the two cases (cases II(i) and II(ii)) by Dirichlet in 1825.  Case II(i) is the case which one of {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, {{mvar|z}} is divided by either 5 and 2.  Case II(ii) is the case which one of {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, {{mvar|z}} is divided by 5 and another one of {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, {{mvar|z}} is divided by 2.  In July 1825, Dirichlet proved the case II(i) for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}}.  In September 1825, Legendre proved the case II(ii) for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}}.  After Legendre's proof, Dirichlet completed the proof for the case II(ii) for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}} by the extended argument for the case II(i).<ref name="Mactutor_1996" />

===Proof for case A===

Case A for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}} can be proven immediately by [[Sophie Germain's theorem]] if the auxiliary prime {{math|''θ'' {{=}} 11}}.  A more methodical proof is as follows.  By [[Fermat's little theorem]],

: {{math|''x''<sup>5</sup> ≡ ''x'' (mod 5)}}
: {{math|''y''<sup>5</sup> ≡ ''y'' (mod 5)}}
: {{math|''z''<sup>5</sup> ≡ ''z'' (mod 5)}}

and therefore

: {{math|''x'' + ''y'' + ''z'' ≡ 0 (mod 5)}}

This equation forces two of the three numbers {{math|''x''}}, {{math|''y''}}, and {{math|''z''}} to be equivalent modulo 5, which can be seen as follows: Since they are indivisible by 5, {{math|''x''}}, {{math|''y''}} and {{math|''z''}} cannot equal 0 modulo 5, and must equal one of four possibilities: 1, −1, 2, or −2.  If they were all different, two would be opposites and their sum modulo 5 would be zero (implying contrary to the assumption of this case that the other one would be 0 modulo 5).

Without loss of generality, {{math|''x''}} and {{math|''y''}} can be designated as the two equivalent numbers modulo 5.  That equivalence implies that

: {{math|''x''<sup>5</sup> ≡ ''y''<sup>5</sup> (mod 25)}} (note change in modulus)
: {{math|−''z''<sup>5</sup> ≡ ''x''<sup>5</sup> + ''y''<sup>5</sup> ≡ 2''x''<sup>5</sup> (mod 25)}}

However, the equation {{math|''x'' ≡ ''y'' (mod 5)}} also implies that

: {{math|−''z'' ≡ ''x'' + ''y'' ≡ 2''x'' (mod 5)}}
: {{math|−''z''<sup>5</sup> ≡ 2<sup>5</sup>''x''<sup>5</sup> ≡ 32''x''<sup>5</sup> (mod 25)}}

Combining the two results and dividing both sides by {{math|''x''<sup>5</sup>}} yields a contradiction

: {{math|2 ≡ 32 (mod 25) ≡ 7}}

Thus, case A for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}} has been proven.

Math. Paris | volume = 82 | pages = 910–913}}</ref>  Alternative proofs were developed by Théophile Pépin<ref>{{cite journal | author = Pépin T | author-link = Théophile Pépin | year = 1876 | title = Impossibilité de l'équation ''x''<sup>7</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''y''<sup>7</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''z''<sup>7</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 | journal = C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris | volume = 82 | pages = 676–679, 743–747}}</ref> and Edmond Maillet.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Maillet E | author-link = Edmond Maillet | year = 1897 | title = Sur l'équation indéterminée ''ax''<sup>''λ''<sup>''t''</sup></sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''by''<sup>''λ''<sup>''t''</sup></sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''cz''<sup>''λ''<sup>''t''</sup></sup> | journal = Assoc. Française Avanc. Sci., Saint-Étienne |series=Série II | volume = 26 | pages = 156–168}}</ref>

=={{math|''n'' {{=}} 6}}, {{math|''n'' {{=}} 10}}, and {{math|''n'' {{=}} 14}}==

Fermat's Last Theorem has also been proven for the exponents {{math|''n'' {{=}} 6}}, {{math|''n'' {{=}} 10}}, and {{math|''n'' {{=}} 14}}.   Proofs for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 6}} have been published by Kausler,<ref name="Kausler_1802" /> [[Axel Thue|Thue]],<ref>{{cite journal | author = Thue A | author-link = Axel Thue | year = 1896 | title = Über die Auflösbarkeit einiger unbestimmter Gleichungen | journal = Det Kongel. Norske Videnskabers Selskabs Skrifter | volume = 7}} Reprinted in ''Selected Mathematical Papers'', pp. 19–30, Oslo:Universitetsforlaget (1977).</ref> Tafelmacher,<ref>{{cite journal | author = Tafelmacher WLA | year = 1897 | title = La ecuación ''x''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''y''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''z''<sup>2</sup>: Una demonstración nueva del teorema de Fermat para el caso de las sestas potencias | journal = Ann. Univ. Chile, Santiago | volume = 97 | pages = 63–80}}</ref> Lind,<ref>{{cite journal | author = Lind B | year = 1909 | title = Einige zahlentheoretische Sätze | journal = Arch. Math. Phys. | volume = 15 | pages = 368–369}}</ref> Kapferer,<ref name="Kapferer_1913" >{{cite journal | author = Kapferer H | year = 1913 | title = Beweis des Fermatschen Satzes für die Exponenten 6 und 10 | journal = Arch. Math. Phys. | volume = 21 | pages = 143–146}}</ref> Swift,<ref>{{cite journal | author = Swift E | year = 1914 | title = Solution to Problem 206 | journal = Amer. Math. Monthly | volume = 21 | pages = 238–239 | doi = 10.2307/2972379 | jstor = 2972379 }}</ref> and Breusch.<ref name="Breusch_1960" >{{cite journal | doi = 10.2307/3029800 | author = Breusch R | author-link = Robert Breusch | year = 1960 | title = A simple proof of Fermat's last theorem for ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;6, ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;10 | jstor = 3029800 | journal = Math. Mag. | volume = 33 | issue = 5 | pages = 279–281}}</ref>  Similarly, [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet|Dirichlet]]<ref>{{cite journal | author = Dirichlet PGL | author-link = Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet | year = 1832 | title = Démonstration du théorème de Fermat pour le cas des 14<sup>e</sup> puissances | journal = J. Reine Angew. Math. | volume = 9 | pages = 390–393}} Reprinted in ''Werke'', vol. I, pp. 189–194, Berlin:G. Reimer (1889); reprinted New York:Chelsea (1969).</ref> and [[Guy Terjanian|Terjanian]]<ref>{{cite journal | author = Terjanian G | author-link = Guy Terjanian | year = 1974 | title= L'équation ''x''<sup>14</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''y''<sup>14</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''z''<sup>14</sup> en nombres entiers | journal = Bull. Sci. Math. |series=Série 2 | volume = 98 | pages = 91–95}}</ref> each proved the case {{math|''n'' {{=}} 14}}, while Kapferer<ref name="Kapferer_1913" /> and Breusch<ref name="Breusch_1960" /> each proved the case {{math|''n'' {{=}} 10}}.  Strictly speaking, these proofs are unnecessary, since these cases follow from the proofs for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 3}}, {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}}, {{math|''n'' {{=}} 7}}, respectively.  Nevertheless, the reasoning of these even-exponent proofs differs from their odd-exponent counterparts.  Dirichlet's proof for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 14}} was published in 1832, before Lamé's 1839 proof for {{math|''n'' {{=}} 7}}.
